original_meaning_en: Body grime; dead skin that exfoliates
original_meaning_es: Mugre corporal; piel muerta que se exfolia
meaning_in_use_en: Accumulated dirt on skin, especially in children
meaning_in_use_es: Mugre acumulada en la piel, especialmente en niños
encoded_social_meaning_en: Working-class / lower-middle-class child; plays outside, barefoot. Absent in upper-class contexts ('that kid is just sweaty')
encoded_social_meaning_es: Clase media-baja; niño que juega en calle, a patapelá. Ausente en clase alta ('ese niño solo está sudado')
typical_context_en: Before bath time, said by mothers/grandmothers: 'go get that piñén off'
typical_context_es: Antes del baño: 'a sacarse el piñén'
functional_translation_en: Body grime / dirt crust (no exact cultural equivalent)
cultural_notes_en: The term encodes a body that labors and plays outdoors, without daily hygiene as a privilege. Its absence in upper-class vocabulary is itself significant.
cultural_notes_es: El término codifica un cuerpo que trabaja y juega afuera, sin la higiene diaria como privilegio. Su ausencia en el vocabulario de clase alta es en sí misma significativa.

claims.verification_note: Attested via native speaker experience and family use across generations. Lexicographic verification against Augusta (1916) and Catrileo (1996) pending. 'Piñán' rejected as documented variant — likely transcription artifact in corpus collection, not an attested alternate form.

original_meaning_en: Mountain lion / lion of the mountain
meaning_in_use_en: The animal; also internationally known as a sports brand — almost nobody knows the word is Mapuche
meaning_in_use_es: El animal; también marca deportiva internacional — casi nadie sabe que la palabra es mapuche
encoded_social_meaning_en: Global brand appropriation of indigenous vocabulary without attribution or acknowledgment
encoded_social_meaning_es: Apropiación de vocabulario indígena por marca global sin atribución ni reconocimiento
typical_context_en: Referring to the animal, or the sports brand
typical_context_es: Al referirse al animal o a la marca deportiva
cultural_notes_en: Paradigmatic case of invisible indigenous origin — the word travels the world with its Mapuche roots erased. One of the most globally recognized words of Mapudungún, recognized precisely because its origin has been made invisible.
cultural_notes_es: Caso paradigmático de origen indígena invisible — la palabra viaja el mundo con sus raíces mapuche borradas. Una de las palabras del mapudungún más reconocidas globalmente, reconocida precisamente porque su origen ha sido invisibilizado.

sources: Zúñiga (2000) — consulted, does not list puma as headword; confirms tra.pi.al 'lion' in phonological examples
claims.verification_note: Widely cited as Mapuche origin in popular and encyclopedic sources. Academic lexicographic confirmation against Augusta (1916) and Catrileo (1996) pending. The animal's historical range overlaps with Mapuche territory, supporting plausibility.

meaning_in_use_en: Gossip; social drama involving third parties; 'he said / she said' entanglement
meaning_in_use_es: Chisme; enredo social; 'que dijo / que no dijo' entre personas
encoded_social_meaning_en: Semantic degradation of a communal indigenous practice into a marker of social toxicity — visible trace of colonial linguistic violence
encoded_social_meaning_es: Degradación semántica de una práctica indígena comunitaria hacia marcador de toxicidad social — huella visible de violencia lingüística colonial
typical_context_en: 'Se armó un cahuín' (drama broke out); 'no metas cahuín' (don't stir the pot)
functional_translation_en: Gossip / drama / stirring the pot (no exact equivalent)
cultural_notes_en: The semantic shift from sacred ritual to petty gossip encodes the colonial displacement of Mapuche culture within everyday Chilean Spanish. The shift itself is the analytically significant datum, regardless of whether the original Mapudungún meaning is fully confirmed.
cultural_notes_es: El desplazamiento semántico de ritual sagrado a chisme codifica el desplazamiento colonial de la cultura mapuche en el español chileno cotidiano. El desplazamiento en sí es el dato analíticamente significativo.

claims.claim_text: Original meaning in Mapudungún was communal/ritual gathering
claims.verification_note: The chilenismo meaning (gossip/drama) is well-attested in Chilean popular use and multiple dictionaries of chilenismos. The original Mapudungún ritual meaning requires confirmation in Augusta (1916) or Catrileo (1996). The semantic shift — from collective sacred practice to individual social toxicity — is the core analytical claim and holds regardless of etymological confirmation.

original_meaning_en: ñuño = dandelion; -a = place suffix → 'place of dandelions'
original_meaning_es: ñuño = diente de león; -a = sufijo de lugar → 'lugar de los dientes de león'
meaning_in_use_en: Name of a commune in Santiago; no floral meaning survives in everyday use
meaning_in_use_es: Nombre de una comuna de Santiago; el significado floral no sobrevive en el uso cotidiano
encoded_social_meaning_en: Indigenous place names persist in urban maps while the culture that named them is systematically displaced — the city remembers the word but erases the people
encoded_social_meaning_es: Los topónimos indígenas persisten en mapas urbanos mientras la cultura que los nombró es desplazada — la ciudad recuerda la palabra pero borra a la gente
typical_context_es: Línea de metro, direcciones, referencias municipales
functional_translation_en: Ñuñoa (untranslatable proper noun; etymological gloss: 'dandelion place')
cultural_notes_en: Paradigmatic case of toponymic fossilization: Mapuche ecological geography survives as an administrative label, stripped of its original ecological and cultural meaning.
cultural_notes_es: Caso paradigmático de fosilización toponímica: la geografía ecológica mapuche sobrevive como etiqueta administrativa, despojada de su significado ecológico y cultural original.

claims.claim_text: ñuño = dandelion in Mapudungún; -a = locative suffix meaning 'place of'
sources: Zúñiga (2000) — confirms locative suffix pattern (-ntu derives 'place characterized by X'); does not list ñuño as headword
claims.verification_note: The locative suffix pattern is confirmed in Zúñiga (2000): -ntu derives nouns referring to a place characterized by the presence of something (e.g. kura-ntu 'stony land', milla-ntu 'place where there is gold'). Whether -a functions identically requires confirmation in Augusta (1916). The botanical meaning of ñuño (dandelion) requires lexicographic verification.

original_meaning_en: Edible red seaweed (Pyropia columbina); pre-Hispanic coastal food source
original_meaning_es: Alga roja comestible (Pyropia columbina); alimento costero prehispánico
meaning_in_use_en: (1) The seaweed, consumed in soups and stews, sold as 'pan de luche' in southern markets; (2) hopscotch-like children's game drawn on the ground
meaning_in_use_es: (1) El alga, consumida en guisos y cazuelas, vendida como 'pan de luche' en el sur; (2) el juego infantil similar al rayuela dibujado en el suelo
encoded_social_meaning_en: Double meaning connects coastal indigenous food culture with urban childhood play — both uses are disappearing in younger generations
encoded_social_meaning_es: El doble significado conecta la cultura alimentaria indígena costera con el juego infantil urbano — ambos usos están desapareciendo en generaciones jóvenes
typical_context_en: 'Vamos a jugar luche' / '¿Compraste luche en la feria?'
typical_context_es: 'Vamos a jugar luche' / '¿Compraste luche en la feria?'
cultural_notes_en: Rare case of one indigenous-origin word covering both a food and a game. Possible connection between the shape of the seaweed and the grid drawn on the ground — not confirmed, but analytically interesting as potential case of metaphorical extension.
cultural_notes_es: Caso raro de una palabra de origen indígena que cubre tanto un alimento como un juego. Posible conexión entre la forma del alga y la cuadrícula dibujada en el suelo — sin confirmar, pero analíticamente interesante como posible extensión metafórica.
source: S.A.A. corpus (native speaker); scientific verification: SUBPESCA/FIPA

sources: SUBPESCA/FIPA biological survey of macroalgae, IX and XIV Regions
claims.verification_note: Confirmed across independent scientific sources. Common misattribution to Ulva lactuca (sea lettuce) corrected: luche = Pyropia columbina, not Ulva lactuca.

claims.claim_text: Linguistic origin of the word luche (Mapudungún or Quechua)
claims.verification_note: Origin not yet confirmed in primary sources. Possible Mapudungún or Quechua etymology; the polysemy (seaweed + game) may reflect independent naming or metaphorical extension. Requires consultation of Augusta (1916) and comparative Quechua dictionaries. Marked disputed rather than unverified because the origin itself is genuinely uncertain, not merely unconfirmed.

original_meaning_es: cocha = agua/lago + yuyo = hierba/maleza → 'hierba del agua'
meaning_in_use_en: Large brown seaweed (Durvillaea antarctica); staple food of Chilean coastal and working-class cuisine
meaning_in_use_es: Alga parda grande (Durvillaea antarctica); alimento base de la cocina costera y popular chilena
encoded_social_meaning_en: Associated with working-class and rural coastal diet; historically coded as 'poor people's food,' now being revalorized as superfood — a class arc visible in a single ingredient
encoded_social_meaning_es: Asociado a la dieta popular y costera; históricamente codificado como 'comida de pobres,' ahora revalorizado como superalimento — un arco de clase visible en un solo ingrediente
typical_context_en: 'Cazuela de cochayuyo'; sold dried and pressed in coastal markets from Coquimbo to Magallanes
typical_context_es: 'Cazuela de cochayuyo'; vendido seco y prensado en mercados costeros de Coquimbo a Magallanes
functional_translation_en: Bull kelp / cochayuyo (no exact English common name; Durvillaea antarctica)
cultural_notes_en: Quechua origin reveals the Andean trade networks that shaped Chilean coastal vocabulary — this word traveled from inland lake cultures to the Pacific coast. The revalorization arc (poor food → superfood) is itself a sociolinguistic event worth tracking.
cultural_notes_es: El origen quechua revela las redes de intercambio andinas que moldearon el vocabulario costero chileno — esta palabra viajó desde culturas lacustres del interior hasta la costa del Pacífico. El arco de revalorización (comida pobre → superalimento) es en sí mismo un evento sociolingüístico.
source: S.A.A. corpus (native speaker); scientific verification: SUBPESCA/FIPA, QUELP.cl

claims.claim_text: Scientific identification: Durvillaea antarctica (and D. incurvata)
sources: Von Suhr 1839 (original scientific description, via QUELP.cl)
claims.verification_note: Confirmed across multiple independent scientific sources. Note: Chilean genetic studies (post-2016) distinguish two species — D. antarctica (Guaitecas to Magallanes) and D. incurvata (north of Guaitecas) — both called cochayuyo in common use. Morphologically similar; the common name covers both.

sources: Zúñiga (2000) — confirms Quechua loanwords in Mapudungún (e.g. kawitu 'bed' from Ayacucho Quechua kawitu); cochayuyo not listed
claims.verification_note: The morphological analysis (cocha + yuyo) is internally consistent with Quechua word-formation patterns documented in the literature. Zúñiga (2000) confirms the pattern of Quechua loanwords entering Mapudungún. Formal attestation in an Ayacucho Quechua dictionary pending.
